lines.say: Here's a puzzle. Your qubit reads zero every time, and you want it to read one.
Picture the qubit, our quantum bit, as an arrow. Up means zero, and down means one.
To change it, we use a gate, which turns the arrow without stretching it.
Our first gate is called X, and it's like flipping a pancake.
Flip the pan, and the top of the pancake ends up on the bottom.
Flip it again, and you're right back where you started.
X does the same to the arrow, spinning it half a turn around a line from left to right.
The arrow pointing up at zero lands pointing down at one.
That's the not gate of ordinary computers: it swaps zero and one every time, with no chance involved.
Do X twice, and two half turns make a full turn, so you're back home.
Here the pancake falls short. It's always one side up, but our arrow can also point in between.
Say it leans toward the top, so it reads zero eight times out of ten.
X still makes its half turn, so now it leans low and reads one eight times out of ten.
X has swapped how much zero and how much one the arrow holds.
And X doesn't read the qubit and then flip it. It turns the whole arrow, lean and all.
In symbols, we call up ket zero and down ket one, and X swaps them.
So remember, gates turn the arrow, and X is the half turn that swaps zero and one.
